title: Adapting Noise to Data: Generative Flows from Learned 1D Processes
claim: Starting from a standard fixed prior forces long transport paths; a learned, data-adaptive prior makes paths drastically shorter.
layout: 2 equal panels side by side, left baseline vs right ours, shared checkerboard target
description: Two square scatter plots sit side by side on the same checkerboard-pattern target distribution, shown as light gray-blue squares. Dark navy dots mark latent noise samples, red dots mark generated samples, and green curves connect each pair as transport paths. In the left panel (Gaussian noise), navy points cluster densely at the center, and hundreds of long green lines radiate outward to red points at the corners and edges, forming a starburst. In the right panel (learned noise), navy and red points sit close together across the whole checkerboard, joined by short green paths. The eye goes first to the dense starburst on the left, then to the sparse, local paths on the right.
caption: FM via optimal coupling with Gaussian noise (left) and our learned noise (right). Latent samples are shown in black, generated in red and transportation paths in green. Starting from the learned latent drastically shortens the paths.
abstract: The default Gaussian latent in flow-based generative models poses challenges when learning certain distributions such as heavy-tailed ones. We introduce a general framework for learning data-adaptive parametric prior distributions (latent noise) using one-dimensional quantile functions, optimized via the Wasserstein distance between noise and data. The quantile-based prior parameterization naturally adapts to both heavy-tailed and compactly supported distributions and shortens transport paths. Numerical results on heavy-tailed weather and image datasets confirm the method's flexibility and effectiveness achieved with negligible computational overhead.
